messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane Haumia is a 65-year-old widowed Māori man working as a project manager for a mid-sized construction firm in Auckland-born but now based in Honolulu, where he relocated following his wife's death several years ago. He presented to an outpatient psychology clinic reporting significant distress, sleep disruption, and what he described as an inability to "get out from under" an experience that had occurred nearly three years prior. His PCL-5 score of 46 placed him firmly in the clinical range, and across the first two sessions a coherent and painful picture emerged.

The precipitating event was his youngest daughter Aroha's sudden collapse at home from a severe asthma attack when she was nine years old. Tane had been the only adult present. He recalled watching her lips turn blue as she struggled to draw breath, her small chest heaving with a desperate, laboured rhythm he could not stop. He had called 911 and attempted to follow the dispatcher's instructions, but by the time paramedics arrived she had lost consciousness. She survived, but spent four days in the paediatric intensive care unit before stabilising. For Tane, those four days — and especially the twenty minutes alone with her before help arrived — became the fixed point around which his entire inner world reorganised.

In the weeks following Aroha's discharge, Tane found himself returning obsessively to what he had done and, more precisely, what he believed he had failed to do. He had come to believe, with a certainty that resisted all counter-evidence, that his slowness in recognising the severity of her symptoms had caused the crisis to escalate. He told himself he should have known — should have acted faster, kept better medications in the house, been more vigilant. The conviction that he had failed to protect his daughter calcified into a broader self-doubt: he could no longer trust his own judgment in any situation that carried stakes. This cluster of self-blame and perceived failure did not remain contained to his private thoughts. It began to colour how he perceived the world around him, making ordinary situations feel saturated with the potential for catastrophe. When a work deliverable ran behind schedule or a subcontractor didn't return a call promptly, Tane found himself certain that something had gone wrong — that delay meant disaster, in the same way that his own delay had nearly cost Aroha her life. His body kept pace with his mind: his heart would race, his chest would tighten, and on the worst occasions he would notice his own breathing becoming shallow and laboured — a sensation that pulled him instantly back to the living room floor, to Aroha's face.

It was these physical echoes that proved most destabilising. Any encounter with breathlessness, his own or another's, acted as a direct portal to the original scene. At work, when a colleague returned from a run and stood panting in the corridor, Tane had to excuse himself. He began avoiding the annual occupational health checks his employer required, finding reasons to reschedule, then simply not booking them at all. He stopped visiting Aroha's paediatrician with her, delegating that role to her older sister. Hospitals, ambulances glimpsed on the highway, even the antiseptic smell of a pharmacy — all of it he routed around. To manage the intrusive imagery that broke through regardless, he kept his mind in constant motion: long hours at the construction site, podcasts running through the night, volunteer work on weekends. He told himself this was coping. What it was, in practice, was a way of never sitting still long enough to examine the belief that he was a man who could not be trusted to keep the people he loved safe. Because he never examined that belief, it never softened. And because it never softened, every reminder of the event — every breathless colleague, every delayed email, every routine medical form — arrived carrying its full freight of threat.

What finally brought Tane to seek help was a mandatory pre-employment medical required for a new project contract. He sat in the waiting room, heard a child coughing in the next bay, and walked out before his name was called. Standing in the car park, he realised he had not seen a doctor himself in nearly three years. What he feared most, he said quietly in session, was that he would never stop waiting for the next thing to go wrong. What he hoped for, with considerably less certainty, was that he might one day be able to trust himself again.
